en: Book 1: The First Section, titled "The Common. Chapter 1: Now, the Compendium of the Treatise.
Section 1.
1.1.1 Homage to Dharma, Artha, and Kāma. 1.1.2 To those [deities] who are the subject matter of this treatise. 1.1.3 And to the teachers who have made known their respective systems. Thus.
1.1.4 Because of its connection with that.

1.1.5 For Prajāpati, having created living beings, first taught them—by means of a hundred thousand chapters—the means for accomplishing the three goals of life (trivarga) as the basis for their stability.
1.1.6 Manu Svāyambhuva composed a separate work based on a portion of that [text], concerning the subject of dharma.
1.1.7 Bṛhaspati [composed] the section on the acquisition of wealth. 1.1.8 And Nandin, a follower of Mahādeva, proclaimed a separate *Kāmasūtra* consisting of one thousand chapters.
1.1.9 Śvetaketu, the son of Uddālaka, abridged that very work into five hundred chapters.

1.1.10 However, Bābhravya Pāñcāla further abridged that very same work by one hundred and fifty chapters into seven sections (*adhikaraṇa*): [1] *Sādhāraṇa*, [2] *Sāṃprayogika*, [3] *Kanyāsaṃprayuktaka*, [4] *Bhāryādhikārika*, [5] *Pāradārika*, [6] *Vaiśika*, and [7] *Aupaniṣadika*.

1.1.11 Dattaka composed the sixth book, the *Vaiśika*, by the command of the courtesans of Pāṭaliputra. 1.1.12 Following that tradition, Cārāyaṇa expounded the *Sādhāraṇa* (General) section; Suvarṇanābha, the *Sāṃprayogika* (On Sexual Union);
Ghoṭakamukha, the *Kanyāsaṃprayuktaka* (On Courting Maidens); Gonardīya, the *Bhāryādhikārika* (On the Duties of a Wife); and Goṇikāputra, the *Pāradārika* (On Adultery).
"Kucumāra [composed] the *Aupaniṣadika*.

(1.1.13) Thus, having been composed in fragments by many teachers, that treatise became nearly lost. (1.1.14) Among those, because the portions of the treatise composed by Dattaka and others were merely partial, and because the work of Bābhravya was [considered] "great," [it was difficult to recover].

Because it is to be studied, this *Kāmasūtra* has been composed in a concise form with few words, summarizing its entire subject matter. 1.1.15 Its table of contents, arranged by chapters (*prakaraṇa*), sections (*adhikaraṇa*), and topics (*samuddeśa*), is as follows: 1.1.16 A summary of the treatise; the attainment of the three aims of life (*trivarga*); the enumeration of the sciences (*vidyā*); and the conduct of the urban dweller (*nāgaraka*).

An investigation of the hero, his companions, and the female messenger. Thus concludes the first general section (*adhikaraṇa*), which consists of five chapters (*adhyāya*) and five sub-sections (*prakaraṇa*).

1.1.17: Establishing the stages of sexual union (*ratāvasthāpana*) according to the measure [of the woman], the time, and her disposition; specific types of affection (*prīti-viśeṣāḥ*); considerations regarding embracing (*āliṅgana-vicārāḥ*); varieties of kissing (*cumbana-vikalpāḥ*); types of scratching with the nails and biting (*nakharadana-jātayaḥ*); methods for cutting with the teeth (*daśana-cchedya-vidhayaḥ*); regional practices (*deśyā upacārāḥ*); modes of coitus (*saṃveśana-prakārāḥ*); wonderful sexual acts (*citra-ratāni*); and the application of wrestling (*prahaṇa-yogaḥ*).

The second book, concerning sexual union (*sāṃprayogika*), consists of ten chapters and seventeen sections: those [positions] involving the man, the commencement with whistling sounds (*sītkṛta*), the male role (*puruṣāyita*), the approaches of the man, the superior position (*aupariṣṭaka*), the beginning and end of sexual intercourse, the specific varieties of sexual acts, and the lovers' quarrel (*praṇaya-kalaha*).
Thus, there are ten chapters and seventeen sections in total.

1.1.18 The third book, *Kanyāsaṃprayuktaka* (Concerning the Union with a Maiden), consists of five chapters and nine sections: 1. The selection [of a suitor]; 2. The determination of the relationship; 3. Gaining the confidence of the maiden; 4. Approaches toward a young girl; 5. Indicating intentions through gestures and appearance; 6. The pursuit by a single man; 7. Winning over the one to be approached; 8. The maiden’s response to the pursuit; and 9. The union for marriage. Thus ends the third book. There are five chapters and nine sections.

1.1.19 The conduct of the woman who wanders alone; the conduct toward co-wives by one traveling abroad; the conduct toward the elder wife; the conduct toward the younger wife; the conduct toward a remarried woman; the conduct toward an unfortunate wife; the conduct regarding women of the harem; and the man’s treatment toward many wives—this concludes the fourth book, titled "Concerning Wives," which consists of two chapters and eight sections.

1.1.20 The Establishment of the Character of Women and Men; Causes of Aversion; Men Accomplished with Women; Women Difficult to Win Without Effort; Causes of Acquaintance; Advances; Examination of Disposition; Duties of the Female Messenger; Love by Command of the Master; Concerning the Harem; Concerning Women Protected by a Husband—thus concludes the fifth book on Adultery, consisting of six chapters and ten sections.

1.1.21 The sixth book, *Vaiśika* (Concerning the Courtesan), consists of: considerations regarding a man who may be approached; the reasons for going to him; the method of winning him over; compliance with the beloved; means of acquiring wealth; signs of detachment; the conduct of a detached man; methods of expulsion; the restoration of a broken relationship; specific gains; deliberation on profit, loss, consequences, and doubt; and the distinctions between types of courtesans.
The seventh book, *Aupaniṣadika*, consists of two chapters and six sections:

1. making attractive (*subhaga-karaṇa*), 2. bringing under control (*vaśī-karaṇa*), 3. aphrodisiacs (*vṛṣya-yogāḥ*), 4. restoring lost passion (*naṣṭa-rāga-pratyānayana*), 5. methods for increasing [virility] (*vṛddhi-vidhayaḥ*), and 6. various other applications (*citrāś ca yogāḥ*). Thus, there are two chapters and six sections.
1.1.23 Thus, there are thirty-six chapters, sixty-four topics (*prakaraṇa*), seven sections (*adhikaraṇa*), and one thousand six hundred and fifty verses; such is the summary of the treatise.
1.1.24 Having stated this summary, its detailed exposition will now be proclaimed; for in this world, the learned desire discourse that is both concise and comprehensive.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Compendium of the Treatise," in the first general section of the *Kāmasūtra* composed by the venerable Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Two: Now begins the second chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Three Aims of Life" (*trivarga*).
Section 2a) Anuṣṭhāna 1.2.1:
A man has a lifespan of a hundred years; having divided this time, he should pursue the three aims of life—which are interconnected and do not obstruct one another—without allowing them to conflict.
1.2.2 In childhood, [one should pursue] matters such as the acquisition of knowledge;
1.2.3 in youth, desire; 1.2.4 and in old age, dharma and liberation.
1.2.5 Or, because life is impermanent, he may practice [the observances] as circumstances permit. 1.2.6 However, [he should observe] celibacy until the acquisition of knowledge. b) Awakening:
1.2.7 Because it is not worldly...

Dharma consists in the instigation of those who have not yet engaged in actions—such as ignorance and the like—by means of the scripture, because it has a visible purpose; and likewise, the restraint from meat-eating and other such acts already in practice by means of the scripture alone, because they are worldly and have a visible purpose.
(1.2.8) One should understand this from the Veda and from the consensus of those who know Dharma.
1.2.9 Wealth (*artha*) consists of the acquisition of knowledge, land, gold, cattle, grain, household utensils, equipment, friends, and so forth, as well as the increase of what has been acquired.
1.2.10 This [is understood] from the conduct of officials and from merchants who know the conventions of commerce.
1.2.11 Desire (*kāma*) is the engagement of the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—presided over by the mind joined with the self—with their respective objects in accordance with one's inclination.

1.2.12 However, because its object is a particular kind of touch, the comprehension of the object—which is accompanied by imagined pleasure and is productive of results—is primarily termed *kāma* (desire). 1.2.13 One should learn that [subject] from the *Kāmasūtra* and from the assemblies of cultured people (*nāgarika*).
1.2.14 Among these [sources], each preceding one is more authoritative than the following.

1.2.15 Wealth (*artha*) belongs to the king, because the course of worldly life is rooted in it; and it belongs to the courtesan as well—thus is the attainment of the three aims of life (*trivarga*). c) Attainment:

1.2.16 Since *dharma* is not of this world, a scripture (*śāstra*) that explains it is appropriate. Because the accomplishment of wealth depends upon means, the attainment of those means comes from scripture.
1.2.17 However, the teachers maintain that even among animals, because sexual desire arises spontaneously and is constant, there is no need for instruction by a treatise.
1.2.18 Because the union of man and woman is dependent upon another, it requires a means.
1.2.19 And Vātsyāyana holds that this acquisition of the means is derived from the *Kāmasūtra*.

1.2.20 Furthermore, because there is no obstruction among those born of animal wombs, and because sexual union with females occurs as long as necessary during their fertile period, and because these activities are not preceded by conscious deliberation, [there is no sin].
Skillful means (*upāya*) is the condition (*pratyaya*).
1.2.21 One should not practice [meritorious] dharmas, because their fruit is yet to come and because they involve uncertainty.
1.2.22 For what wise person would cast away what is already in hand to seek what belongs to another?
1.2.23 A pigeon today is better than a peacock tomorrow. 1.2.24 A certain kārṣāpaṇa is better than a doubtful niṣka; thus say the Lokāyatikas. 1.2.25 [This is] not [the view] of the Śāstra.
Because of the existence of suspicion, because the results of malevolent spells and curses are sometimes observed, because the movement of the circle of constellations, the moon, the sun, stars,

and planets is seen to proceed as if with prior intelligence for the sake of the world, because the course of worldly life is characterized by the stability of the conduct of the castes and stages of life, and because one observes the relinquishing of seed already in hand for the sake of a future crop— one should practice [renunciation].

"Regarding the phrase 'the dharmas,' Vātsyāyana says: one should not pursue objects of sense. For even if these are practiced with great effort, they may never come to pass; yet, even without being practiced, they might occur by chance. (1.2.26)
1.2.27 All that is caused by time.

1.2.28 For it is time alone that establishes men in prosperity or adversity, victory or defeat, and pleasure or pain. 1.2.29 By time Bali was made Indra; by time he was deposed; and by time alone he shall be made [Indra] once again—thus say the proponents of time as the cause (*kālakāraṇikāḥ*).

1.2.30 Because all activities are preceded by human effort (*puruṣakāra*), the means (*upāya*) is the basis for conviction (*pratyaya*). 1.2.31 Even for a matter that is certain to occur, it is only through the employment of means that it comes to pass; there is no prosperity for one who is devoid of action—so says Vātsyāyana. 1.2.32 One should not pursue desires, because they are antagonistic to dharma and artha, which are the two primary goals, as well as to other virtuous things. [One should avoid] association with people of no purpose, improper resolve, impurity, and...
And these produce for a person in the future:
1.2.33 negligence, levity, and lack of confidence.
And [the state of] being an object of perception. 1.2.34 Furthermore, it is heard that many hosts who fell under the power of desire were indeed destroyed.
1.2.35 Just as the Bhoja king named Dāṇḍakya perished along with his kinsmen and kingdom because he, out of lust, lusted after a Brahmin’s daughter;

1.2.36 And the King of the Gods [Indra] for Ahalyā, the exceedingly powerful Kīcaka for Draupadī, Rāvaṇa for Sītā, and many others besides— those who contemplate worldly affairs see that these were destroyed by falling under the power of desire.
1.2.37 For desires have the nature of sustenance because they are the cause of the maintenance of the body; and they are the fruit of dharma and artha.

1.2.38 But one must understand [the truth] regarding them just as one does regarding faults. For it is not the case that because there are beggars, cooking pots are not placed on the fire; nor is it the case that because there are wild animals, barley is not sown—so says Vātsyāyana.
1.2.39 There are verses on this point:

A man who pursues wealth, pleasure, and virtue in this manner enjoys ultimate happiness, free from all thorns, both in this world and the next. 1.2.40 Regarding that action in which no doubt arises as to what might happen in the hereafter, and which is neither destructive of wealth nor contrary to happiness—in that, the learned are established.

1.2.40v2: One should perform even that task which accomplishes the three aims of life (*trivarga*), whether for both or for one alone; however, one should not perform a task that serves a single purpose while obstructing two others.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Three Aims of Life" (*trivarga-pratipatti*), in the first book, the General Section (*sādhāraṇa*), of the *Kāmasūtra* composed by the venerable Vātsyāyana.
Chapter 3: Now begins the third chapter, titled "The Exposition of Learning" (*vidyāsamuddeśa*).
Section 3.1.3.1:
Without neglecting the time for the sciences that are limbs of dharma and artha, a man should study the Kāmasūtra and its auxiliary sciences.
1.3.2 Before puberty, a woman [is under her father's authority], and after marriage, she is under the will of her husband. 1.3.3 Because women lack the capacity for the study of the scriptures,
the teachers maintain that instruction for women in this treatise is useless.

1.3.4 Vātsyāyana, however, maintains that the inclusion of these [arts] is for the sake of their practical application (*prayoga*), since such application is preceded by the study of the treatises (*śāstra*).
1.3.5 That is not so; for it is not only here [in this context]. Indeed, in all the world, there are only a few who know the treatises, whereas practical application pertains to all people.
1.3.6 And even though the treatise may be remote, it alone is the cause of practical application.
1.3.7 Even those who are not grammarians, such as ritualists (*yājñika*), employ modifications (*ūha*) in sacrifices, thinking, "Grammar exists.
1.3.8 Thinking, "Astronomy (*jyotiṣa*) exists," they perform their rites on auspicious days.
1.3.9 Likewise, horse-riders and elephant-riders [train] horses and elephants [respectively].
Even those who have mastered the treatises are disciplined.
Just as subjects in distant provinces do not overstep the bounds of propriety when they know "the King exists," so it is with this.
Indeed, there are courtesans, princesses, and daughters of high officials whose intellects have been refined by the study of the treatises.

1.3.12 Therefore, a woman should learn the entire treatise or a portion of it in secret from a trustworthy person through practical application. 1.3.13 A maiden should practice in secret and alone the sixty-four arts (catuḥṣaṣṭika-yogāḥ) intended for repeated application.
1.3.14 However, the teachers of maidens are those who have themselves engaged in sexual union with men.
A foster-sister who has grown up together;

likewise, a female friend with whom one speaks freely and without reserve; a maternal aunt of the same age; a trusted elderly maidservant who occupies that position; a female mendicant with whom one was previously acquainted; and a sister, due to the application of mutual trust.
1.3.15 Singing (1), instrumental music (2), dancing (3), and painting (4).
(5) the cutting of decorative patterns, (6) the various arrangements of rice and flower garlands, and (7) the spreading of flower carpets.
(8) the application of red lac to the teeth and garments, (9) the work of inlaying gemstones into the floor, and (10) the arrangement of beds.
(11) water music,
(12) water-splashing,
and (13) various yogic practices.
(14) the conceptualizations of weaving garlands, (15) the arrangement of crests and tiaras, and (16) the application of cosmetics and dress.
(17) the fashioning of ear-ornaments, (18) the preparation of perfumes, and (19) the arrangement of jewelry.
(20) illusions, (21) the art of Kaucumāra,
and (22) manual dexterity.
(23) the preparation of various vegetable soups and food preparations; (24) the compounding of syrups, juices, condiments, and fermented liquors; (25) the arts of needlework and weaving.
(26) playing with threads, (27) playing musical instruments such as the lute and the hand-drum, (28) riddles.
(29) the practice of making images, (30) the application of difficult-to-pronounce words, and (31) the recitation of books.
(32) the study of drama and narrative tales; (33) the completion of poetic stanzas with missing parts; (34) the various techniques for weaving plaits and working with cane.
(35) the crafts of the carpenter,
(36) wood-carving, (37) the science of architecture.
(38) Examination of Silver, (39) Discourse on the Elements, (40) Knowledge of the Luster and Mines of Gems.
(41) The applications of the science of tree-life; (42) the method for fighting rams, cocks, and quails; (43) the training of parrots and mynas to speak.
(44) Skill in rubbing the body, massaging, and dressing the hair;
(45) speaking in ciphers and using hand gestures; (46) various forms of foreign or unintelligible speech.
(47) knowledge of regional dialects,
(48) the Flower-Cart [magical display], (49) knowledge of signs.
yantra-mātṛkā (50), dhāraṇa-mātṛkā (51), sampāṭhyam (52).
(53) mental composition of poetry, (54) lexicography, (55) knowledge of prosody.
(56) The ritual of action, (57) the applications of deception, (58) the concealment of clothing.
(59) a particular kind of gambling, (60) the game of dice,
(61) children’s toys.
(62) those pertaining to discipline, (63) those pertaining to victory, and (64) those pertaining to physical exercise.

"Knowledge of the sciences" refers to the sixty-four *aṅgavidyās* (auxiliary sciences), which are branches of the *Kāmasūtra*. 1.3.16 There is another set of sixty-four, known as the *pāñcālikī*; having understood its applications, we shall describe them in the section on sexual union (*sāṃprayogika*), because love consists of that. 1.3.17 A courtesan who is distinguished by these [sciences], and endowed with good character, beauty, and virtues, earns the title of *gaṇikā* and a place in the assembly of people.
1.3.18 Always honored by the king and praised by those possessed of virtue, she becomes one who is sought after, worthy of approach, and an object of admiration.

1.3.19 A princess skilled in yoga, as well as the daughter of a high minister, brings even a husband with a harem of a thousand women under her own control. 1.3.20 Likewise, even when separated from her husband and having fallen into terrible distress, she lives in happiness through these sciences, even in a foreign land.

1.3.21 A man who is skilled in the arts, eloquent, and a maker of flatteries—even if he has not been previously acquainted—quickly wins the hearts of women. 1.3.22 Good fortune arises simply from the mastery of the arts; however, their application depends upon place and time, and may or may not be possible.
1.3c Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Exposition of Knowledge," in the first book, the General Section, of the *Kāmasūtra* composed by Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Four: On the Conduct of the Urban Dwellers (*nāgaraka*).
Section Four.

1.4.1 Having acquired knowledge and entered the state of a householder with wealth obtained through gifts, conquest, purchase, or inheritance—whether ancestral, self-acquired, or both—he should conduct himself according to the way of life of a *nāgaraka* (urban gentleman).
1.4.2 His residence should be in a city, a port-city, a market town, or a large settlement inhabited by virtuous people; or it may be wherever his livelihood leads him.
1.4.3 There, he should have a house built near a water source, provided with groves of trees, with its various functional areas clearly partitioned, and containing two dwelling chambers.

1.4.4 And in the outer dwelling room, there should be a bed with very smooth pillows on both sides, sloping down in the middle, and covered with a white upper sheet. There should also be a couch. At its head-end, there should be a place for a seat of grass (kūrca) and a raised platform (vedikā). There, one should apply ointment and wear garlands during the remainder of the night.

There should be a box for rice-grains, a pouch for fragrant substances, citron peels, and betel leaves. On the floor is a spittoon. A lute hangs from a peg. There is a painted board, a case for brushes, and whatever books there may be, as well as garlands of *kuraṇṭaka* flowers. Not far away on the floor is a circular rug with a headrest, and a gaming board and a dice board.
And outside of it were cages for sporting birds. In a secluded spot was the workshop of carpenters and woodworkers, as well as other places for recreation.
In the grove of trees there were swings and hammocks spread out in the pleasant shade. And there was a raised platform on a leveled plot of ground.
The arrangement of the dwelling is in bloom. 1.4.5 Having risen in the morning and performed his fixed duties, having taken up his tooth-cleanser, and having taken a moderate amount of ointment,
incense, and a garland, and having applied beeswax and lac, he looks at his face in a mirror and takes up mouth-perfume.
One should attend to one's duties while using betel.

1.4.6 Bathing should be performed daily. The second [application] is for removing dirt; the third is soap-powder; the fourth is for longevity; and the fifth or tenth is for restoring vitality—this is not deficient. Furthermore, by doing so continuously, the sweat of the armpits is removed.
1.4.7 Eating during the forenoon and afternoon; and in the evening, according to Ārāyaṇa.
1.4.8 After eating, activities such as making parrots and mainas talk; cockfights, ramfights, and various games of skill; activities dependent on the *pīṭhamarda*, the *viṭa*, and the *vidūṣaka*;
and sleeping during the day.
1.4.9 In the afternoon, after he has finished his adornment, there are social gatherings and diversions.

1.4.10 And at nightfall, there are musical performances. At the conclusion of these, in his bedchamber which has been decorated and perfumed with fragrant incense, he awaits the visiting women upon the couch of his companion.
1.4.11 Sending female messengers or going oneself.

1.4.12 And for those who have arrived, the approaches of the companion consist of captivating conversation and services. 1.4.13 [The approaches] of those whose finery has been washed away by the rain are difficult...
For women who set out for their lovers during the day, there should be either self-adornment or attendance by friends; this constitutes the daily routine.
(1.4.14) She should organize gatherings of jars, social assemblies, drinking parties, excursions to gardens, poetic riddles, and games.
(1.4.15) On a fixed day of every fortnight or month, a regular assembly should be held in the house of Sarasvatī for those appointed to participate.

1.4.16 Visitors who are actors and performers should provide them with a spectacle. On the second day, they shall invariably receive honor from them. Thereafter, their attendance may be according to their inclination, or they may be dismissed. During times of misfortune or festival, they shall act as one body with one another.
1.4.17 And for visitors who have formed a group, there shall be both honoring and assistance.
1.4.17c This is the rule for the group (*gaṇa*).
1.4.18 By this, the vessels that have been prepared in honor of various specific deities are explained.

1.4.19 A social gathering (*goṣṭhī*) is the taking of seats by those of equal learning, intellect, character, wealth, and age, together with courtesans, in a courtesan’s house, in an assembly hall, or in the residence of one of them, accompanied by appropriate conversation.
1.4.20 And therein, they engage in poetic competitions or artistic competitions.

1.4.21 In those [competitions], those who are brilliant, beloved by the people, and worthy of honor are honored; and those who are equal in affection are invited as participants. 1.4.22 Furthermore, drinking parties are held in each other’s residences.

1.4.23 There, courtesans should serve and they themselves should drink honey-wine, maireya-wine, and surā-wine, accompanied by various salts, fruits, leafy vegetables, bitter and pungent items, and sour condiments.
1.4.24 By this, the procedure for going to a pleasure garden is explained.
1.4.25 [This should be done] in the forenoon itself.

Adorned and mounted on horses, they should go accompanied by courtesans and followed by attendants. Having enjoyed the daily excursion there, and having passed the time with cockfights, gambling, spectacles, and agreeable diversions, they should return in the same manner in the afternoon, bearing the marks of their enjoyment.
1.4.26 By this, the going for water-sports in the summer, when the pools have been prepared with embankments, is explained.
1.4.27 The Night of the Yakṣas; the Kaumudī Vigil; the Spring Festival.

1.4.28 They should perform for the people various distinguished games, such as the breaking of the *sahakāra* (mango) tree, the eating of raw meat (*abhyūṣa*), the eating of lotus stalks (*bisakhādikā*), the "new leaf" game (*navapattrikā*), the "water-scream" (*udakakṣveḍikā*), the "procession of the Pāñcālas," the "single *śālmali* tree," the "kadamba-tree battles," and other such regional (*deśya*) and royal (*māhimānya*) pastimes.
Thus end the games played in groups.
1.4.29 And those played by a solitary person are possible through the power of wealth.
1.4.30 By this, the conduct of the courtesan and of the heroine together with her female friends and the city-dwellers is explained.

1.4.31 But the *pīṭhamarda* (the court jester) is one who possesses no wealth other than his body; he is provided with only a few items such as jasmine, soap-berry, and astringent powders; having come from a respectable region and being skilled in the arts, he maintains himself by means of instruction in those arts within social gatherings and in conduct appropriate for the courtesan's quarter.
1.4.32 But he who has enjoyed his wealth yet remains virtuous, who is highly esteemed by his wife, in the harem, and in social assemblies, and who subsists upon him, is a *viṭa*.
1.4.33 One who possesses knowledge of only a single branch [of learning], who is playful and trustworthy, is a *vidūṣaka* or a *vaihāsika*.
1.4.34 These are the ministers of courtesans and gallants, appointed to manage peace and war.
1.4.35 By these [rules], female mendicants, those skilled in the arts, shaven-headed women, low-caste women, and elderly courtesans are explained.
1.4.36 And so is the village-dweller.

Having encouraged those who are born with discernment and curiosity, he should describe the conduct of city-dwellers, inspire faith in them, and imitate that very conduct himself. He should initiate social gatherings, win over people through association,
assist them in their undertakings, and provide them with benefits.

1.4.36c Thus concludes the conduct of the urbanite (*nāgaraka*). 1.4.37v One who narrates a story in social gatherings using neither exclusively Sanskrit nor exclusively the local dialect will be highly esteemed in the world.
1.4.38v A wise man should not descend into a social gathering that is detested by the world, one that spreads through mere license, or one whose nature is to cause injury to others.
1.4.39v By conducting himself in society together with a circle of companions who follow the ways of the world and whose sole purpose is amusement, the wise man attains success in the world.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Conduct of the Urban Dandy," in the first section, "General Principles," of the *Kāmasūtra* composed by the venerable Vātsyāyana.
Chapter Five: An Examination of the Hero’s Assistants and the Duties of the Messenger.
Section 5.1.5.1:
Sexual desire exists among the four castes;
it is [regulated] according to caste and according to the scriptures.
When practiced with a woman who has had another husband previously, it results in sons, fame, and worldly success.

1.5.2 The opposite of that occurs when [the practice is performed] with women of superior caste or those already taken by others. It is forbidden with women of inferior caste who have been cast out from their community. With courtesans and remarried women, however, it is neither prescribed nor forbidden, because it serves merely for pleasure.
1.5.3 In this regard, there are three types of heroines: the maiden (*kanyā*), the remarried woman (*punarbhū*), and the courtesan (*veśyā*).
1.5.4 Goṇikāputra maintains that there is a fourth type, the "occasional" (*pākṣikī*), who, though married to another, [is available] due to other circumstances.

3.4.27 And when she has come for the purpose of frequent meetings, he should increase the social gathering. 3.4.28 Even with other women, he should apply himself more and more for the sake of gaining her confidence, but he must not speak disparagingly.
3.4.29 For even one whose passion has gone far away does not succeed with maidens through disparagement; so says Ghoṭakamukha.
3.4.30 But when she considers herself highly proficient, then indeed he should begin. 3.4.31 At twilight, at night, and in the darkness, women have little apprehension;

they are intent upon sexual union and full of passion. They do not reject a man. Therefore, it is the common saying that she should be approached at such a time. 3.4.32 However, regarding the advances of a single man... [text fragment]

When the opportunity arises, she should have her brought onto her lap by a nurse’s daughter or a female friend who has grasped the meaning of the matter and is acting as an intermediary to communicate that purpose to her; thereafter, she should apply the pressure as previously described.
3.4.33 Or, he should assign one of his own female attendants to her from the very beginning as a friend.

3.4.34 At a sacrifice, a wedding, a journey, a festival, a time of misfortune, or when people are occupied with spectacles— he should approach her when she is alone, having observed her gestures and appearance and tested her feelings on various such occasions.
3.4.35 Vātsyāyana maintains that women who have been seen [to respond] do not turn away when approached at the proper place and time; thus ends the section on the pursuit by a single man.
28. Thus ends the section on the pursuit by a single man.
Section 29: Even a maiden who possesses good qualities, though she be of noble birth and devoid of wealth, if she is not sought in marriage by suitors of equal status;
or one who is separated from her parents, or residing in the family of her paternal kinsmen, having reached the age of puberty, may herself desire to take the hand [of a husband].
3.4.37 But she should, out of affection for her son, attach herself to one who is virtuous, capable, and pleasant to behold.
3.4.38 Or to one whom she might think [would please] her mother and father.
Considering that he might also act toward her due to his own weakness of the senses, she should win him over with pleasant and beneficial attentions and by frequent meetings.
3.4.39 Her mother, together with her female friends and nurses, should turn her toward him.
3.4.40 [She should do so] while holding flowers, perfumes, and betel in her hand.

One should attend upon her at the appropriate time and place. Or, when demonstrating skill in the arts, one should observe propriety in massaging and pressing the head. One should employ conversational topics suited to the inclinations of the person to be won over; in the case of a young girl, one should proceed with the introductory measures as previously described.
3.4.41 Furthermore, she should not herself make advances toward a man even in private. For the teachers maintain that a young woman who makes advances of her own accord loses her good fortune.
3.4.42 However, she may accept advances initiated by him, provided they are consistent with propriety.

And she should not show any sign of transformation. She should accept him with a gentle appearance as if she were unaware [of his intent]. There is forceful seizing of the face. 3.4.44 When being solicited for the cultivation of passion, there is the touching of the secret parts only with difficulty.

3.4.45 Even when requested, she should not reveal herself too openly. Elsewhere [it is said]: 3.4.46 But when she thinks, "He is enamored with me and will not turn away," then she should hasten to unite with him for the sake of liberating herself from her state as a maiden. 3.4.47 And having been released from her maidenhood, she should disclose it to those who are trustworthy.
3.4.47c: Thus is the bringing back (*upāvartana*) of the one to be employed.
Section 30. 3.4.48: And there are verses on this point.

3.4.48 But a maiden being courted should take as her husband one whom she considers a source of happiness—someone who is well-disposed toward her, obedient, and under her influence. 3.4.49 Where a man disregards virtues, beauty, and propriety, she may, out of greed for wealth, take him as her husband even if he has co-wives. 3.4.50 In such a case, a maiden should not be seduced by a suitor who possesses the necessary qualities, is obedient, capable, powerful, and persistent, and who pursues her with various stratagems.

3.4.51 It is better to have a husband who is submissive— even if he is poor, devoid of virtues, and barely able to sustain himself— than one who, though endowed with virtues, is shared by many. 3.4.52 Generally, the wives of the wealthy are numerous and...
Obstacles: Even when external enjoyments are present, those who lack confidence and find pleasure in outward things [are hindered].
(3.4.53v) Furthermore, a man who is base, or even one who is grey-haired, as well as one whose character is to travel to foreign lands, does not deserve to enter into a union.
3.4.54 One who is approached by chance, even if he excels in deceit and gambling, is not fit for union if he has a wife and children.
3.4.55 When the suitors are equal in merit, the one suitor who is chosen as the best is the preferred one; for that excellence in the suitor consists essentially of his affection.

3.4c Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Approaches of a Single Man and the Maiden’s Response to Those Approaches," in the third book, "On the Acquisition of Maidens," of the *Kāmasūtra* composed by Śrī Vātsyāyana.

31. [The Section on the Yoga of Marriage] If she cannot obtain a secluded audience with the maiden, she should approach the foster-sister (*dhātreyikā*), winning her over with things that are pleasant and beneficial. That foster-sister, appearing as if unknown to the hero (*nāyaka*), should win him over by means of his virtues. She should describe the hero’s qualities, which are pleasing to her, most extensively.

3.5.3 One should point out the faults of other suitors that are contrary to her own inclinations. 3.5.4 [One should describe] the virtues of her parents, as well as the lack of discernment, greed, and fickleness of her kinsmen.
3.5.5 And one should mention other maidens of the same caste, such as Śakuntalā and others, who, having obtained husbands through their own ingenuity, have lived happily in union with them.
And he should point out to her examples of women who,
though born in noble families, were oppressed by co-wives, became objects of hatred, suffered in misery, and were abandoned. Furthermore, he should describe her future prospects.
3.5.8 He should describe the unimpeded happiness found in solitary wandering, as well as the hero’s affection for her.
3.5.9 And he should dispel, by means of appropriate reasons, her fear, shame, and anxiety regarding the potential loss of this man who shares her desires.
3.5.10 He should also perform the entire ritual procedure concerning the female messenger.
3.5.11 She should arrange matters so that the hero might take her by force as if she were unaware, thinking, "In this way, she will be perfectly won over.

3.5.12 When she has consented and is staying in the desired location, the hero, having brought fire from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), having spread *kuśa* grass, and having offered oblations according to the traditional rules, should circumambulate [the fire] three times.
3.5.13 Then he should make it known to his mother and father.
3.5.14 For the rule of the teachers is that marriages witnessed by fire are not to be annulled.
3.5.15 And having corrupted her, he should gradually make it known among his own kinsmen.
3.5.16 He should employ such means that her kinsmen, wishing to avoid the family's disgrace and out of fear of punishment, would give her back to him.
3.5.17 And immediately thereafter, he should gratify her kinsmen with affectionate gestures and through the display of passion.

3.5.18 Or he should act by means of the *gāndharva* form of marriage. 3.5.19 If she does not consent, he should win over another woman of the family who moves within the household, with whom he has previously been acquainted and who is well-disposed toward him; through her, he should have her brought to a secluded place under the pretext of some other business.
3.5.20 Then, "the fire from the house of a Vedic scholar"—the rest is the same as before.
3.5.21 When the wedding is near, she should cause her mother to feel regret by pointing out the faults of the bridegroom that she herself had approved of.

3.5.22 Then, with her mother’s consent, having summoned the lover at night to a neighboring house or a lodging-house, [she should perform the rite] with fire from the house of a Vedic scholar; the rest is the same as previously described.

3.5.23 Or, she should win over her brother— whether he is of equal age or addicted to courtesans or other men's wives— by providing assistance in difficult undertakings and by pleasing him with favors; she should keep him attached for a very long time and, at the end, cause him to adopt her own intention.

3.5.24 For generally, young men will even sacrifice their lives for the sake of friends who share their same character, vices, and age. Therefore, she should have her brought there under that very pretext of another task. "Is it endurable?"—this is the same as before.

3.5.25 And on occasions such as the eighth-day moonlight festival, a foster-sister (dhātreyikā) should have her drink an intoxicant and, under the guise of some personal business of her own, lead her to a place where the hero is present and it is endurable. There, she [should...]
"Having violated her while she was unconscious from intoxication"— the rest is the same as before.
3.5.26 "And having kept away the nurse who was alone with her while she was asleep," [and so on].
The phrase "having corrupted her as she was proceeding" is the same as the previous [case].
3.5.27: Having learned that she is going to another village or a garden, the hero, well-prepared with his companions, should abduct the maiden after frightening or killing her guards.
3.5.27c Thus end the types of marriage.
3.5.28v Among these marriages, each preceding one is superior according to the law and established tradition. In the absence of the former, the latter—each succeeding one in turn—should be performed.
3.5.29v Since the fruit of all marriages is mutual affection, even the middle-ranking Gāndharva rite is honored as a virtuous union.

3.5.30 Because it is pleasant, because it involves little distress, because it lacks obstacles in this world, and because it is characterized by affection, the Gāndharva form of marriage is considered the best.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, "Forms of Marriage," in the third section, "On Maidens," of the *Kāmasūtra* composed by the venerable Vātsyāyana. Book 4: The Fourth Section, "Concerning the Wife" (*Bhāryādhikārikam*).

32. [The Chapter on Conduct for a Wife Who Moves Alone] 4.1.1 A wife who moves alone, possessing secret confidence,
should behave toward her husband with favorability as if he were a god.
4.1.2 According to his view, he should take the care of the family upon himself.
4.1.3 And the house should be clean, with its areas well-swept, adorned with various flowers, with a smooth floor surface, and pleasing to the sight.
One should perform the ritual of offerings at the three daily junctures and worship the shrines of the deities;
for Gonardīya maintains that there is nothing else so captivating to the minds of householders as this.
[One should also act] toward teachers, the circle of servants, and the sisters of the leader.
And one should show appropriate respect toward their husbands.
4.1.6 When they have been purified, one should cause them to cultivate plots of green vegetables, clumps of sugarcane, and shrubs of cumin, mustard, *ajamoda*, *śatapuṣpā*, and *tamāla*.
4.1.7 [One should also cause them to cultivate] shrubs of *kubjaka*, *āmalaka*, jasmine (*mallikā*), *jātī*, *kuraṇṭaka*, *navamālikā*, *tagara*, *nandyāvarta*, and *japā*.
Furthermore, one should have many other flowering plants, young *kośīraka* grasses, and *pātālikā* creepers planted, and have charming level ground (*sthaṇḍila*) prepared within the grove of trees.
In the center, one should have a well, a pond, or a long oblong pool excavated.
4.1.9 He should not associate with female mendicants, female ascetics, Jain nuns, unchaste women, female fortune-tellers, or women who practice root-magic.
4.1.10 Regarding food, he should discern: "This is pleasing to him," "this is disliked by him," "this is wholesome," and "this is unwholesome."

4.1.11 Having heard his voice from outside as he approaches the house, she should stand ready in the middle of the dwelling, asking, "What must be done? 4.1.12 Having dismissed the female attendant, she herself should wash his feet.
4.1.13 Furthermore, the hero should not remain in a secluded place for public viewing while devoid of ornaments.
4.1.14 If he is making excessive expenditures or improper expenditures, she should inform him in private.

4.1.15 At a wedding, a marriage, or a sacrifice, she may go with her female friends; she may engage in social gatherings and visit deities when permitted. 4.1.16 In all amusements, she should conduct herself in accordance with his wishes.
4.1.17 She should lie down after him and rise before him.
And there should be the awakening of one who has slept.
4.1.18 And the kitchen should be well-guarded and beautiful to behold.
4.1.19 When the hero has committed an offense, she should not speak excessively with resentment, even if she is somewhat troubled.
4.1.20 However, she may reproach him with words of censure when he is in the midst of his friends or when he is alone; yet she must not be the cause of a fundamental rift.
4.1.21 For there is no other cause for the [suffix] *a* than this, says Gonardīya.
4.1.22 *durvyāhṛtam* (is used in the sense of) "ill-spoken."
One should avoid looking elsewhere while conversing, standing at the doorway to eavesdrop, or conversing in garden groves (*niṣkuṭa*) or secluded places for a long time.
4.1.23 [One should also avoid] perspiration, stains from tooth-cleaning paste, and foul odors...
"And one should perceive odors"—this is the cause for detachment (virāga).
4.1.24 An attire consisting of many ornaments, various flowers and ointments, and garments radiant with various bodily pigments is the "approachable" (ābhigāmika) dress.
4.1.25 Wearing thin, smooth, and few fine silken cloths (dukūla), limited ornaments, and [moderate]...

The scent should not be too overpowering; likewise, the ointment and other white flowers constitute the attire for wandering. 4.1.26 She should personally follow the hero’s vows and fasts by performing them herself. And when she is forbidden [from something], she should withdraw from his words, thinking, "I am not to be persistent in this matter."
4.1.27 And [thefts] of vessels made of clay, split bamboo, wood, leather, or metal, when the time [for their disposal] has arrived;
4.1.28 Likewise, the secret concealment within houses of salt, fats, fragrant substances, pungent goods, vessels, and medicinal herbs that are difficult to obtain.

4.1.29 At the proper time, one should collect the seeds of radish, *kāluka*, *pālaṅkī*, *damanaka*, *āmrātaka*, cucumber, gourd, eggplant, pumpkin, bottle-gourd, *sūraṇa*, *śukanāsā*, *svayaṃguptā*, *tilaparṇikā*, *agnimantha*, garlic, onion, and other such medicinal plants, and sow them at the appropriate season.
4.1.30 One should not disclose one's own essential secrets to others, nor that which has been deliberated with one’s master.
4.1.31 She should excel her co-wives in skill, brilliance, culinary art, dignity, and likewise in her modes of service.
4.1.32 Having calculated the annual income, she should make expenditures corresponding to it.
4.1.33 From the milk remaining after consumption, she should prepare clarified butter, as well as oil and molasses; and she should spin thread from cotton.
The weaving of thread; the collection of carrying-straps, ropes, nooses, and bark-fiber; supervision of threshing and grinding; the utilization of raw grain, husks, chaff, bran, and charcoal;
knowledge of the wages and maintenance of servants; the management of agriculture, cattle-rearing, transport, and equipment;
the supervision of rams, cocks, quails, parrots, starlings, cuckoos, peacocks, monkeys, and wild animals; and the daily calculation of income, expenditure, and savings.
One should know that this is the "instrument" (karaṇa).

4.1.34 Furthermore, there shall be a store of worn-out garments for those of low status; by means of these, whether dyed in various colors or plain, there shall be favor shown to attendants who have performed their duties, gifts given for the sake of honor, or their use elsewhere. 4.1.35
The storage of jars of *surā* liquor and jars of *āsava* spirits, their consumption, their purchase and sale, and the supervision of income and expenditure;
4.1.36 the honoring of leaders and friends in accordance with propriety by giving them garlands, ointments, and betel;
4.1.37 service to one's mother-in-law and father-in-law and dependence upon them.
Speaking in reply is limited;
it consists of engaging in harsh speech and loud laughter, which are dear to them.
One should behave toward one's own loved ones as if they were the beloved of others.
4.1.38 One should not be arrogant regarding enjoyments.
4.1.39 One should show courtesy toward the household servants.
4.1.40 One should not give anything to anyone without first informing the husband.
4.1.41 One should direct the servants in their respective duties and honor them during festivals.
4.1.41c Thus ends the section on the "Woman Who Wanders Alone" (ekacāriṇī-vṛtta).
Section 33: [The Section on Conduct During Absence from Home] (pravāsa-caryā-prakaraṇam).

4.1.42 While her husband is away on a journey, she should wear only auspicious ornaments, be devoted to fasting for the deities, and look after the household while remaining attentive to news from him.
4.1.43 Her bed should be near her elders. She should accomplish whatever tasks they desire. She should exert effort in acquiring and maintaining the objects desired by her husband.
4.1.44 She should spend money according to the requirements of obligatory and occasional rites. She should be intent on completing the tasks he has begun.
4.1.45 She should not visit the family of her kinsmen except on occasions of misfortune or festivals;
even then, she should not remain there for too long, being accompanied by the hero’s attendants.
And the alteration of travel attire.

4.1.46: The performance of fasts by those who have received permission from their elders; the replenishment of resources and the reduction of expenditures according to one's capacity, through the regulated trade of buying and selling overseen by pure attendants acting under orders.
4.1.47 And upon her return, she should first be seen while remaining in her natural state; then there shall be the worship of the deities and the bringing of offerings.
Thus ends the conduct regarding travel (pravāsa-caryā).
4.1.48 And there are two verses on this subject: [The verses follow.]

A woman who desires the welfare of her husband should follow him—whether she be a woman of noble family, a remarried woman, or even a courtesan—if she conducts herself as one devoted to a single man. Women who adhere to virtuous conduct obtain dharma, artha, and likewise kāma, as well as a secure position and a husband free from rivals.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Conduct of a Woman Devoted to One Man and the Conduct During Absence," in the fourth book, *Bhāryādhikārika*, of the *Kāmasūtra* by the venerable Vātsyāyana.
Lesson 2, Second Chapter.
Section 34: [The Section on the Conduct of the Eldest, etc.]

4.2.1 Taking a second wife may occur due to the birth of children characterized by dullness, misconduct, or misfortune; or due to the frequent birth of daughters; or because of the husband’s fickleness.
4.2.2 From the very beginning, she should seek to prevent this by making manifest her devotion, virtuous character, and cleverness. Children.
And she herself should incite her co-wife regarding the husband's lack of affection.

(4.2.3) While being superseded [by a rival], she should ensure her own superior status through the application of her power. (4.2.4) When the rival has arrived, she should look upon her like a sister; and with great effort, she should cause her to perform the evening rites known to the lover. She should pay no heed to any change in her [the rival] caused by good fortune or to her arrogance.
4.2.5 She should overlook her husband when he is being negligent. Where she thinks, "She will understand this matter for herself," there she should instruct her with particular care.
4.2.6 And in private, within the hearing of the hero, she should show her special excellence.
4.2.7 Regarding his children:

There is a distinction: excessive compassion toward the circle of attendants; affection toward the circle of friends; lack of great respect for one's own kinsmen; and excessive deference toward their kinsmen.

4.2.8 However, a woman who has been superseded by many [co-wives] should form an alliance with one who is not separated [from her husband]. 4.2.9 But whichever woman the husband intends to favor excessively, she should incite a quarrel with a former favorite wife.
4.2.10 And then he should show compassion. 4.2.11 He himself should desire to act as one with them, being without dispute and free from malice.
One should act as a female companion (*janī*).
4.2.12 One should console her when she has quarreled with the hero, bolstering her with partiality and support.
4.2.13 And one should increase the quarrel.
4.2.14 Or, having perceived a slight quarrel, she herself should inflame it.
4.2.15 If she thinks that the lover is still conciliatory toward her even now, then she herself should strive for reconciliation.
4.2.15c Thus ends the conduct of the senior wife (*jyeṣṭhā*).
Section 35: 4.2.16 But he should look upon his youngest wife as he does his mother.
4.2.17 One should not enjoy even her inheritance from her relatives without her knowledge. 4.2.18 One should carry out one's own affairs under her supervision.
4.2.19 Having been permitted, she may lie with her husband. 4.2.20 Nor should she report his words to another woman.
4.2.21 She should regard his offspring as superior to her own. 4.2.22 She should attend upon her husband more especially in private.
4.2.23 She should not speak of the suffering she experiences arising from her co-wife’s transformation [of status].
4.2.24 And she should seek to maintain a secret, special mark of respect toward her husband.
4.2.25 She should say, "Indeed, I live by this giving of wholesome food.
4.2.26 But she should not speak of that outwardly out of pride or passion.
4.2.27 For one whose secrets are disclosed incurs the contempt of her husband.
4.2.28 According to Gonardīya, she should conceal her desire for honor out of fear of her elder sister.
4.2.29 He should show compassion toward an elder sister who is unfortunate or childless, and he should cause the lover to show her compassion as well.
4.2.30 But having taken her by force, he should follow the conduct of one who lives alone;
4.2.30c thus ends the conduct of the youngest wife (*kaniṣṭhā*).
Section 36.
4.2.31 But a widow who, due to weakness of her senses, being distressed, should marry again a man endowed with good qualities and wealth is a *punarbhū*.
4.2.32 However, according to the followers of Bābhravya, if she departs from him again of her own free will because he is devoid of merit, she may then desire another.
4.2.33 She, seeking happiness, might indeed find another.
4.2.34 Gonardīya maintains that because there is a totality of pleasure in the enjoyment of [her] qualities, she is therefore superior to him.
4.2.35 Vātsyāyana says it is because she conforms to his own mind.

4.2.36 She should, with her kinsmen, seek from the hero activities that involve the capacity for expenditure, such as [funds for] drinking parties, gardens, religious rites, gifts, friends, and worship. 4.2.37 Or she may, by means of her own resources, maintain his ornaments or her own. 4.2.38 There is no fixed rule regarding gifts given out of affection.

4.2.39 When she departs from her home of her own free will, she shall forfeit everything other than the affectionate gifts given by the hero. However, if she is being expelled, she shall not give up anything at all. 4.2.40 She may enter his house as if she were the mistress.
4.2.41 But with women of noble birth, he should conduct himself with affection.
4.2.42 Through courtesy toward his attendants, he maintains a conduct that is everywhere full of jesting toward his friends; he possesses skill in the arts and superior knowledge.
4.2.43 And in situations where a quarrel might arise, she herself should take notice of the hero.

4.2.44 In private, she should attend to him with the sixty-four arts (*kalā*). She herself should provide for her co-wives. She should give gifts of ornaments to their children. Toward them, she should behave as toward the master. She should apply cosmetics and adornments without regard for her own dress. She should maintain a disposition for social gatherings, drinking parties, garden excursions, and recreational outings, both among the household staff and her circle of friends.
4.2.44c Thus ends the section on the remarried woman (*punarbhū*). Section 37.

4.2.45 However, she who is unfortunate (*durbhagā*) and oppressed by her co-wives should attend more closely than others to her husband; he should take her under his protection. He should also display his public knowledge of the arts (*kalā*), for [the secrets] of the unfortunate are not revealed.
4.2.46 She should act as a foster-sister to the children of the hero.
4.2.47 Having gained the favor of his friends, she should manifest her devotion to them.
4.2.48 And she should be a leader in religious duties, as well as in vows and fasts.
4.2.49 One should show courtesy toward the attendants, and one should not regard oneself as superior. 4.2.50 On the bed, one should win back his affection by conforming to his habits.
4.2.51 One should neither reproach him nor display any perversity.

4.2.52 And with whichever woman he has quarreled, he may at will bring her back to him. 4.2.53 And whichever woman he desires in secret, he should cause her to meet with this man and keep it concealed.
4.2.54 And so that she maintains her status as a devoted wife...
The hero should not suspect deceit; he should respond accordingly.
(4.2.54c) Thus ends the section on the conduct of the unfortunate woman. Section 38.
4.2.55 One should observe the conduct of the women of the harem within these very same sections.
4.2.56 The chamberlains or senior female attendants should present to them garlands, ointments, and garments, saying, "These were sent by the queens.
4.2.57 Having accepted those, the king should give back their used garlands as a return gift.
4.2.58 And [the king], having adorned himself, should look upon all the women of the inner apartments together during the afternoon.
4.2.59 His conduct toward them should consist of appropriate placement, honor, and deference, according to the time and their individual merit.

And he should engage in humorous conversations. 4.2.60 Immediately after that, he should likewise look upon women who have remarried. 4.2.61 Furthermore, there are courtesans, those from the inner apartments, and actresses.
4.2.62 Their respective positions correspond to the stages previously described.

4.2.63 As for the chamberlains (*vāsakapālīs*), those who attend upon whichever woman has been designated as the favorite, whichever woman’s time with the king has passed, and whichever woman is in her fertile season, shall follow their respective attendants and report to the king when he rises from his daytime bed the ointment marked with the signet ring sent by them, as well as the woman’s fertile season and her status as the current favorite.
4.2.64. Whatever the king may take from there, he shall order a dwelling place for her.

4.2.65. And at festivals, all [the women] shall receive worship and drink according to their rank, as well as at performances of music. 4.2.66. For those who move within the inner apartments, there is no going outside; and for outsiders, there is no entering inside.
Entry [is permitted] except for those whose purity is well-known. And the application of ritual action is untroubled. Thus ends the section on the women of the inner apartments. 4.2.66c.
Section 39. 4.2.67. There are also verses on this point:
4.2.67v. A man, having gathered many wives, should remain impartial toward them; he should not show contempt for them, nor should he tolerate their deceitful behavior.
4.2.68 One should not mention to other women the sexual play or any bodily transformation arising from passion that occurred with one woman, nor any reproach resulting from intimacy.
4.2.69 He should never give women an opportunity for such behavior on account of his wife; rather, he should direct any reproaches they may offer regarding faults toward her alone.

4.2.70 One should please women in this manner: by means of confidential intimacies with one in private, by public honors toward another, and likewise by showing great respect to yet another. 4.2.71 One should win over each individual woman through visits to gardens, sensual enjoyments, gifts, honoring her kinsmen, secret endearments, and acts of affection.
4.2.72 A young woman who has conquered her anger and conducts herself according to the scriptures brings her husband under her control. He [who possesses such a wife]—

"And he supersedes his wives" (4.2c). Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Conduct Toward Co-wives: The Conduct of the Senior Wife, the Conduct of the Junior Wife, the Conduct of the Remarried Woman, the Conduct of the Unfortunate Wife, and the Conduct of the Harem Women; the Man’s Dealing with His Wives," in the fourth book, the *Bhāryādhikārikam*, of the *Kāmasūtra* composed by Vātsyāyana. Book Five: The Adulterous (*Pāradārikam*). *** **Book Five: On Adultery** Chapter One: The Conduct of the Man Who Has Another’s Wife as His Mistress 1.1 The man who has another’s wife as his mistress [The Section on Establishing the Character of Women and Men].
5.1.1 Those who have explained their reasons and have entered into the acceptance of another's position (130).
5.1.2 Regarding them, one should examine from the very beginning whether the matter is yet to be proven, whether it is already understood, its future prospects, and its practical application.
5.1.3 But when one sees [another] moving at will from one place to another, one may take possession of others' belongings for the sake of protecting oneself and one's own body from injury.
5.1.4 There are ten stages of desire (kāma).
5.1.5 [1] Delight of the eye, [2] attachment of the mind, [3] arising of volition, [4] loss of sleep, [5] emaciation, [6] withdrawal from sense objects, [7] loss of shame, [8] madness, [9] fainting.
[10] "Death" refers to their outward signs.

5.1.6 Regarding this, the teachers maintain that one should observe a young woman’s character, truthfulness, purity, tractability, and impetuosity through both her physical form and her characteristics.
5.1.7 Vātsyāyana, however, holds that because physical form and characteristics can be deceptive, the actual conduct of a woman must be understood solely through her gestures and facial expressions.

5.1.8 When a woman sees any man who is radiant, she desires him; likewise, a man also [desires] women. However, Gonikaputra says that they do not proceed [to act] out of mere consideration. 5.1.9 In this regard, there is a distinction concerning women.
5.1.10 A woman does not [abandon] dharma...

She regards the law and indeed desires it; yet, out of regard for her duty, she does not engage [with him]. (5.1.11) Furthermore, even when she desires to act while being pursued by a man due to his own nature, she turns away.
(5.1.12) When pursued again and again, she succeeds.
5.1.13 But a man, out of regard for the stability of righteousness and the conventions of the noble, desists even when he is desirous.
5.1.14 And one who possesses such an understanding does not succeed even when being assailed.
5.1.15 He assails without cause; having assailed, he does not assail again; and when success is achieved, he adopts an attitude of neutrality.
5.1.16 It is a common saying that one disregards what is easily obtained and longs for what is difficult to obtain. Section 40.
5.1.17 Therein, the causes for turning away [from her husband] are as follows:
5.1.18 Affection for another husband; 5.1.19 Desire for offspring.
5.1.20 The state of having passed beyond youth. 5.1.21 Overwhelmed by suffering. 5.1.22 Non-perception due to separation.
5.1.23 "He addresses [him] with contempt" refers to anger. 5.1.24 "Unconjecturable" refers to the abandonment of volitional resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
5.1.25 "He will go"—[this is the beginning of the next section].
"And [the thought] 'my future depends on another'—this is attachment of the mind elsewhere" (5.1.26).
"His outward form is unrestrained"—this is agitation (5.1.27).
"He has entrusted his heart to friends"—this is concern for them.
5.1.28 "He is one who pursues with persistent intensity"—this is the apprehension. 5.1.29 "He is spirited"—this is the trepidation.
5.1.30 "He is of fierce impetuosity or capable"—this is the fear of the doe.
5.1.31 It is a source of shame that a city-dweller (*nāgaraka*) is proficient in the arts (*kalā*).
5.1.32 And it is likewise [shameful] that he is treated with the intimacy of a friend.
5.1.33 It is a cause for resentment that he does not know the proper place and time.

5.1.34 "A ground for humiliation" means a lack of respect. 5.1.35 "Even when summoned, she does not wake up" refers to contempt. 5.1.36 "Slow-moving" and "having dull speed" are terms for an elephant.

5.1.37 Compassion (*anukampā*) is the desire that "may this [suffering] not befall him," arising from being moved by [another's] distress. 5.1.38 Disgust (*nirveda*) arises from perceiving faults within oneself.
5.1.39 Fear that, being discovered, one will be cast out by one's own people.
5.1.40 Disrespect [expressed] as "he has turned grey."
5.1.41 "He is employed by his master; thus he investigates" is the deliberation.
5.1.42 "And there is regard for dharma.
5.1.43 Whatever one might perceive within oneself regarding those [objects], one should determine it from the very beginning.
5.1.44 Those [faults] associated with nobility arise from the increase of passion. 5.1.45 Those born of incapacity arise from the failure to demonstrate the means.
5.1.46 Those caused by high esteem arise from excessive familiarity.
5.1.47: [One should offer] those things caused by humiliation out of one's skillfulness.
5.1.48: Those arising from that humiliation [should be offered] through prostration.
5.1.49 [The sections] concerning those filled with fear are up to [the rule on] taking heart. Section 41.
5.1.50 These men, however, are for the most part accomplished; one who knows the *Kāmasūtra* and is skilled in storytelling and narration [is so] from childhood.

One who has been associated [with her] since childhood, whose youth has fully developed, who has gained confidence through play and other activities, who is accustomed to performing errands and engaging in appropriate conversation, who has previously acted as a messenger for a lover, who knows her secrets, who is requested by a high-born friend, who is secretly associated with her,
who is renowned for his good fortune, who grew up together with her, who is a neighbor, who is devoted to love, and who is of such a character.
The attendant, cherished by the foster-mother, a youth of nine years, accustomed to spectacles, gardens, and giving, known as Vṛṣa,
possessed of proven prowess, daring, and heroic, surpassing his master in learning, beauty, virtues, and enjoyments, and distinguished by costly dress and refined manners. (Section 42)

5.1.51 Just as one should perceive the attainment of success for oneself, so too should one do for women. 5.1.52 However, these women are not accomplished through mere effort; rather, they are won over simply by application. She stands at the doorway.
She gazes upon the royal highway from the palace. She arranges social gatherings at the house of a young neighbor. She watches constantly.
She was watched by him as she looked toward his side.
She was superseded by a co-wife without cause; she hated her husband and was detested by him; she lacked protection and was childless.

5.1.53 [The following women are suitable for the practice of *kuṭṭanī*]: one who is constantly occupied with her kinsmen and family; one whose children have died; one who organizes social gatherings (*goṣṭhī*); one who fosters friendships; the wife of an actor or singer; a young widow; a poor woman who enjoys many pleasures; the wife of an elder brother who has many brothers-in-law; a highly proud woman whose husband is inferior;
and one who is distressed by her husband’s stupidity despite her own pride in her own skill.
Especially out of greed.

5.1.54 At that time, she had been somehow warded off with effort during her maidenhood, yet she was not [successfully] resisted when he made his advances. She was equal to him in intellect, character, intelligence, understanding, and disposition; she was naturally partial [to him], and—

"She has been insulted because of a transgression, surpassed by women of equal beauty, and her husband is away. She is one whose husband is jealous, foul-smelling, fastidious, impotent, procrastinating, a coward, hunchbacked, dwarf, deformed, a jeweler, vulgar, malodorous, diseased, or old.
Regarding this, there are two verses (5.1.55).

5.1.55 Desire, born of one’s own nature and nourished by action, becomes firm and imperishable when its agitation has been purified by the intellect. 5.1.56 Having recognized his own success and inferred the signs of women, the man who eliminates the causes for their aversion achieves mastery over women. [The Section on the Application of Causes for Familiarization] 5.2.1 Just as a maiden is to be won by one’s own direct advances (*abhiyoga*), she is not so won by means of a female messenger (*dūtī*). However, the teachers maintain that the wives of others, possessing subtle dispositions, are to be won by a messenger and not by oneself. 5.2.2 In every case, where one has the power to do so, self-effort is more appropriate than employing another.

Vātsyāyana maintains that because it serves as a means of access, the employment of a female messenger (*dūtī*) is appropriate. (5.2.3) Those who are bold for the first time, as well as those who speak without restraint, should be won over by themselves; those who are the opposite of this should be approached through a messenger. (137)
And the statement "by means of a messenger" is a general rule.
5.2.4 However, one who intends to make an advance himself should first establish a familiarity [with her].
5.2.5 This familiarity may be either natural or effortful.

5.2.6 Natural [signals] occur when she is near her own home; those resulting from effort occur when she is near the houses of friends, kinsmen, high officials, or physicians, or during weddings, sacrifices, festivals, calamities, garden visits, and the like.

5.2.7 Regarding her appearance, there is constant gazing with expressive gestures, the arranging of her hair, the clipping of her nails, the polishing of her ornaments, the pressing of her lower lip, and various playful movements while she watches with her female companions, all of which are connected to him.
Furthermore, there are conversations directed toward others, the disclosure of [one's own] renunciation or enjoyment, yawning with a contraction of the limbs while seated on a friend’s lap,
the raising of a single eyebrow, slow speech, listening to her words, engaging in seemingly useless conversation with a child or another person directed toward her,
and expressing one's own desires to her under the pretext of speaking about someone else.

Kissing and embracing the child, giving him betel with the tongue, and touching the region of his jaw with the forefinger— these should be performed as appropriate and according to the occasion. 5.2.8 Furthermore, when the child has come into her lap, she should fondle him and give and take his toys.
Because of his proximity, one should engage him in conversation; having gained the favor of people capable of conversing with him,

one should arrange for his coming and going along with his business and its related matters, and take recourse in this [method] while he remains unaware— this indeed is the discourse on the *Kāmasūtra*.

5.2.9 When their acquaintance has become established, he should place deposits and trusts in her hand. He should then withdraw portions of these from time to time, day by day and moment by moment. 5.2.10 He should provide her with fragrant substances and betel nuts.
5.2.11 He should cause her to join in confidential conversations and sit on secluded seats together with his own wives.

5.2.12 This is for the purpose of constant sight and for the purpose of gaining her confidence. [He should employ her] among goldsmiths, jewelers, lapidaries, and dyers of indigo, safflower, and the like.
And when she desires sensual pleasure, he himself should strive to accomplish it for her along with those who are under his control.
5.2.13 For one who is devoted to carrying out that [work], there should be frequent meetings known to the public over a long period of time.
5.2.14 And during those [meetings], there should also be consideration of other tasks.

5.2.15 She should demonstrate that her proficiency, the application, the acquisition, the means, and the specialized knowledge regarding whatever action, substance, or skill she desires are under her own control.

5.2.16 She should engage in debate with her and her attendants concerning worldly activities previously undertaken and the examination of the qualities of substances. 5.2.17 Regarding the stakes established therein, she should appoint her as an arbiter in those matters.
5.2.18 But if he disputes with her, he should say, "It was something quite extraordinary.
5.2.18c These are the causes for gaining familiarity.

5.2.19 One should approach a woman who has already become acquainted with him and whose internal feelings have been revealed through gestures, using strategic means, as if she were a maiden. Generally, the approaches there are subtle because maidens have not yet had sexual union. With other women, one should employ those same means openly, because they have already had sexual union.
5.2.20 When her outward appearance has been revealed and her true nature disclosed during the course of their enjoyment, he should make use of her personal belongings.

5.2.21 Among these, there should be costly perfume, an upper garment, a flower, and a finger-ring. Having taken betel from her hand, he may request a flower from her hair when he is about to depart for a social gathering.
5.2.22 In that situation, he should give her a precious perfume that is desirable, marked with the signs of his own nails and teeth, and accompanied by a significant gesture.
5.2.23 By means of increasingly intense advances, one should dispel her timidity.

5.2.24 The advances consist of: proceeding gradually to a secluded place; embracing; kissing; taking and giving betel; exchanging objects at the conclusion of the gift-giving; and touching the private parts.
5.2.25 And where one woman has been approached, one should not approach another there.
5.2.26 In that regard, she should win over a woman who has experienced objects of pleasure with the elderly and who is won over by endearments.
5.2.27 There are two verses on this subject:
5.2.27v Wherever the hero—the husband of that woman—is seen to be moving about elsewhere, one should not disregard any woman there, even if she is easily accessible.
5.2.28 A wise man, knowing his own capacity for success, should not attempt to seduce a woman who is suspicious, guarded, fearful, or one who has a mother-in-law.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Causes of Acquaintance and Advances," in the fifth book, "On Adultery," of the *Kāmasūtra* composed by Vātsyāyana.

5.3.1 One who makes advances should examine the woman's conduct; through that, her disposition is examined. He should also accept her advances. 5.3.2 If she does not disclose his secret counsel, he should win her over by means of a female messenger. 5.3.3 If she does not accept his advances but continues to associate with him, one should recognize her as being divided in mind; he should win her over gradually.

5.3.4a: Having accepted his advances, she should appear adorned with special finery and go to meet him again in a secluded place; one should know her to be capable of being taken by force. 5.3.5: She who endures even many advances and gives herself away before long is one who accepts [the suitor] dryly; she is to be won by breaking off their acquaintance.
5.3.6 Because the human species is characterized by the impermanence of the mind.

5.3.7 Even when approached, she avoids him and does not become intimate with him, nor does she reject him, due to her pride and sense of self-importance regarding that [other] man. Because of her extreme familiarity [with him], she is difficult to win over. One should win her over through a female messenger who knows her vital secrets (*marma-jñā*).
5.3.8 If, when being assailed, she rebuffs him with harshness, she is to be disregarded.
5.3.9 But even after he has been harsh, he should win her over by uniting her with affection.
5.3.10 She who tolerates physical contact for a specific reason but does not acknowledge it—she is to be won over either by winning her over completely through a divided mind or by constant patience.

5.3.11 When she is lying nearby, he should pretend to sleep and place his hand upon her. She, too, as if asleep, remains indifferent; but if she is awake, she pushes him away, desiring further advances. 5.3.12 By this, the placing of one foot upon the other [of the woman] is explained. 5.3.13 When that has proceeded, he should again initiate the embrace of one who is pretending to sleep.

5.3.14 One should recognize that she who, unable to endure it, rises [in anger] on the second day, yet returns to her natural state and seeks a reconciliation, as one who desires union. However, if she remains invisible, she is to be won over by means of a female messenger (*dūtī*). 5.3.15 Even if she has not been seen for a long time, if she remains in her natural state and meets [the lover], he should approach her once she has displayed the signs of her condition and revealed her true feelings. 5.3.16 [The man should act] as follows... (text fragment)

Though not formally appointed, she makes her intentions known. She shows herself in solitude. She speaks with a trembling voice and in a faltering tone. Her fingers, hands, and feet become perspiring, as does her face. She invites the hero to massage her head and to press her thighs. (5.3.17) Acting as a masseuse for one in distress, while massaging with one hand, she makes contact and embraces him with her other arm. She displays an air of feigned astonishment.

5.3.18 Or, blinded by sleep, she remains touching him with her thighs and even her arms. She lets a portion of her forehead rest upon his thighs. When employed to massage the base of his thighs, she does not resist. She places one hand motionless right there. And when he squeezes her with a grasp of his limbs, she removes it only after a long time.
5.3.19 Having thus accepted the advances of the lover, she approaches him again on the second day for the purpose of massaging him.
5.3.20 She does not embrace him excessively, nor does she avoid him. 5.3.21 In a secluded place, she reveals her affection without any apparent motive.
"Secretly" means in a concealed place.
5.3.22 If she is one who is enjoyed by a nearby attendant, and even when summoned remains just as she was, she is to be won over by a female messenger who knows her vital points.
5.3.23 But if she turns away, she is to be scrutinized.
5.3.23c Thus concludes the examination of internal disposition (bhāva-parīkṣā).
5.3.24 There are also verses on this subject:
5.3.24v First one should establish familiarity, and then engage in conversation; interspersed with conversation, one should mutually observe their outward behavior.

5.3.25 If, by means of a reply, he perceives the acceptance of his gesture (*ākāra*), then the man, free from fear, should make his advances toward the woman. 5.3.26 A woman who first reveals her own inner state through her gesture should be approached immediately, even at the very first sight.
5.3.27 But she who, when addressed gently, clearly gives a positive response, should be known as one who is accomplished at that very moment and is longing for sexual union.
5.3.28 This subtle method is prescribed for women who are self-possessed, not yet experienced, and those who are being examined; indeed, these women are clearly established [as targets].
Thus ends the third chapter, "Examination of Dispositions," in the fifth section, "On Adultery," of the *Kāmasūtra* composed by Śrī Vātsyāyana.
