5.4.1 However, once her gestures and facial expressions have been revealed, he should approach her through a female messenger— she who is rarely seen and with whom he has no prior acquaintance.
5.4.2 Having gained her confidence by conforming to her character, he should win her over through the artifice of storytelling, methods for becoming beloved, and accounts of worldly affairs.
He should delight her with stories of poets and stories of adulterers, and by praising her beauty, discernment, skill, and character.
(5.4.3) He should instill in her a sense of regret, saying, "How can such a person as you have a husband like this?
(5.4.4) And he should say, "O fortunate one, it is not even fitting for you to perform the duties of a servant."

5.4.5 When she is in his presence, he should speak at length about his own sluggishness, jealousy, deceit, ingratitude, lack of sexual desire, miserliness, fickleness, and whatever other hidden faults he may have; likewise, he should speak even more excessively regarding her own similar qualities when they are present.
5.4.6 And by means of whichever fault he perceives her to be distressed, he should penetrate her heart through that very same point.
5.4.7 When she is a deer, then there is no fault in her being a hare. 5.4.8 By this very same [principle], the cases of the mare and the female elephant are also explained.

5.4.9 But Goṇikāputra says that one should approach a woman who has committed her first bold act and whose feelings are subtle only after having gained the confidence of the heroine herself, acting as a messenger.
5.4.10 She should recount the hero’s conduct, his devotion, and his desires. 5.4.11 And when her affection has been fully aroused, she should skillfully speak thus regarding the body of the matter:
5.4.12 “Listen, O fortunate one, to this wonderful thing: having seen you there, that hero, the son of such-and-such a lineage, is experiencing a madness of the heart. By nature he is...”

She should describe him as follows: "The prince was once elsewhere a practitioner of asceticism who had never experienced such things before; therefore, it is now possible for him to even experience death.
(5.4.13) There, having observed a favorable change in his speech, face, and gaze on the second day, she should resume the conversation.
(5.4.14) While he is listening, she should also tell other worldly stories, such as those of Ahalyāvimāraka and Śakuntalā, which are appropriate to the situation.

5.4.15 She should describe the man's virility, his sixty-four arts of knowledge, his good fortune, and his praiseworthiness; she should also describe his secret union with her, whether it has already occurred or has not yet happened before.
5.4.16 And she should observe his outward appearance.
5.4.17 Having seen her with a smile, he addresses her.
5.4.18 And he invites her to sit.
5.4.19 He asks: "Where did you stay? Where did you sleep? Where did you eat? Where did you wander? Or what was done?"
5.4.20 She reveals herself in a secluded place.
5.4.21 She engages him in storytelling. 5.4.22 While reflecting, she sighs and yawns.
5.4.23 And she bestows a gift of affection.
5.4.24 She remembers [him] during sacrifices and festivals. 5.4.25 She dismisses him with the intention of seeing him again.
5.4.26 Being one who speaks well, she says: "What is this?"
She connects the conversation by saying, "Please speak what is auspicious.
(5.4.27) She points out the faults of the hero related to his deceit and fickleness. (5.4.28) And she herself [mentions] their previous meeting and his application to the conversation.
While she is speaking, he longs for what is being said by her. 5.4.29 And when the hero’s desires are being told,
he laughs at what is called "contempt," yet he does not speak out against it.
5.4.30 The female messenger should reinforce her, who has already revealed her intentions, with tokens of recognition from the hero.
5.4.31 But if she is not yet acquainted with him, the messenger should win her over by describing his virtues and stories of his affection.
5.4.32 Auddālaki maintains that there can be no role for a messenger between two people who are neither acquainted nor have seen each other’s appearance.

5.4.33 According to the followers of Bābhravya, [the *pluta* vowel] occurs even between two vowels that have not been previously recited together (*asaṃstuta*), provided they appear in a combined form (*saṃsṛṣṭākāra*).
5.4.34 Goṇikāputra maintains that it occurs even between two vowels that have been previously recited together (*saṃstuta*), provided they do not appear in a combined form (*asaṃsṛṣṭākāra*).
5.4.35 Vātsyāyana maintains that even between two people who are not well-acquainted and have not seen each other, [intimacy may arise] through the mediation of a female messenger.
5.4.36 He should show her heart-captivating gifts sent by him, such as betel, ointment, a garland, a ring, or a garment.
5.4.37 On these [garments], there should be nail-marks, tooth-marks, and various other signs corresponding to the lover's actions.

5.4.42 But according to the followers of Bābhravya, he [the king] may do so during visits to deities, on expeditions, in garden sports, when descending into water, at weddings, sacrifices, calamities, festivals, in the event of a fire, during a disturbance caused by thieves, when the countryside mounts its chariots, at spectacles, and in various such affairs.

5.4.45 The specific types of female messengers (*dūtī*) are: the one with full authority (*nisṛṣṭārthā*), the one with limited authority (*parimitārthā*), the bearer of a letter (*patrahārī*), the self-appointed messenger (*svayaṃdūtī*), the foolish messenger (*mūḍhadūtī*), the wife-messenger (*bhāryādūtī*), the mute messenger (*mūkadūtī*), and the wind-messenger (*vātadūtī*).
5.4.46 The *nisṛṣṭārthā* is she who, having understood the purpose of both the hero and the heroine according to their wishes, accomplishes the task through her own intelligence.

5.4.59 One should employ her very same [messenger] to deliver replies on her behalf.

5.4.61 Or, a young girl or a female attendant...

Section 47: [The Section on the Desires of Lords] 5.5.1 Neither kings nor their high ministers have the right to enter the private residences of others. For their conduct is observed by the public and followed by them.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, "following the beloved" is *saṃdhāna* (reconciliation). "Rejoining the broken" (*viśīrṇa-pratisaṃdhāna*) is the *vaiśika* (the art of courtesans). Because it possesses that purpose along with the remaining two [sections], it is called *Vaiśika*.
